nameStory: The Pink Arum gets its name from its gorgeous pink funnel-shaped flower that looks like a colorful trumpet. It's also called the pink calla lily, though it's not a true lily at all - the name comes from the Greek word 'kalos' meaning beautiful, which perfectly describes these elegant blooms.
description: Pink Arum is a striking ornamental plant that grows from a bulb-like structure underground. It produces one distinctive funnel-shaped pink flower that looks almost like it's made of smooth, waxy plastic. The plant typically reaches 12-18 inches tall with arrow-shaped green leaves that have a glossy, almost rubbery texture. This is a garden escape that's extremely rare in New England's wild spaces.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single pink funnel-shaped bloom that feels smooth and waxy to the touch, like thick paper or plastic, with a yellow spike (called a spadix) poking up from the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Arrow or heart-shaped leaves with a glossy, rubbery texture that feel thick and substantial when you touch them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a neat clump from underground bulbs, typically 12-18 inches tall, with leaves and flowers emerging directly from the base

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy flower stems that feel sturdy and succulent-like, often with a slight bend or curve

habitat: Extremely rare in New England - only one observation recorded! When found, it's typically an escape from cultivation in disturbed areas near gardens, roadsides, or abandoned homesites. Prefers moist, well-drained soil and partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the ground in late spring, followed by the distinctive pink flowers in late spring to early summer.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with the waxy pink blooms at their most vibrant. Leaves remain green and glossy throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for dormancy. Flowers have long since faded.
seasonality.winter: Plant is completely dormant underground with no visible above-ground parts remaining.

funFact: Despite being called a 'lily,' Pink Arum is actually more closely related to skunk cabbage and jack-in-the-pulpit - they're all in the Arum family and share that distinctive flower structure with a central spike surrounded by a colorful bract!
confusionNotes: The waxy, funnel-shaped pink flower is so distinctive that it's hard to confuse with anything else in New England. The closest would be other calla lilies in gardens, but those are typically white or yellow rather than pink.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'calla lily' creates confusion because this isn't a true lily at all - true lilies are in a completely different plant family. This naming mix-up happens with many ornamental plants where common names reflect appearance rather than actual botanical relationships.
compareHints: Pink Arum is the only Zantedeschia species recorded in New England. Compared to other Arum family members like Jack-in-the-pulpit or skunk cabbage, it has that distinctive smooth, waxy funnel flower instead of the hooded spathe, and much more refined, garden-like appearance rather than the wild, robust look of our native arums.
